cards.title: Source Daniel
cards.text: Fictional profile: Daniel is 24, Christian and a care worker. He says, “I believe every person is made in the image of God, so everyone deserves dignity.” He chose care work over a better-paid job.

return_check.prompt: Give one key belief in Christianity and one in Humanism, then identify a difference.
return_check.answer: For example, Christians believe in one God as Trinity; Humanists do not believe in a god and regard this as our only life. Their beliefs about God differ.

source_lessons.outcome: Identify a key belief in two worldviews and explain one similarity or difference.

return_check.prompt: What is authority in RE? Explain how a sacred text or conscience could guide a choice.
return_check.answer: A trusted source of guidance. Amira may use the Qur’an to guide honesty; a person may consult conscience about right and wrong.

source_lessons.outcome: Recognise a source of authority or meaning and explain how it may guide a believer or non- religious person.

return_check.prompt: Name a shared value shown by the church mediation group and the mosque open day. Give a source detail.
return_check.answer: Peace, welcome or dialogue. Mediation helps neighbours resolve conflict; the open day helps neighbours meet.

source_lessons.outcome: Explain how a festival or shared value can bring people together and identify one value linked to peace.

return_check.prompt: In “Daniel values dignity. For example, he chose care work. This lets him care for others”, identify the evidence and explain what the final sentence adds.
return_check.answer: “For example, he chose care work” is evidence; the last sentence links that choice to the value of dignity and explains how.

source_lessons.outcome: Write or give a structured explanation using a point, evidence/example and explanation.

return_check.prompt: Compare the Christian and Humanist remembrance responses. Use a point, a detail from each source and an explanation of a similarity and a difference.
return_check.answer: Both remember people and value peace. The Christian source prays and believes people are in God’s care; the Humanist source does not pray and values memories and preventing war. They share remembrance and hope for peace while their beliefs and practices differ.

source_lessons.outcome: Compare how two worldviews may respond to remembrance or peace.

staff_html:
Teacher card

Evidence, belief and choices

Outcome: Use evidence from the half-term to explain how beliefs and worldviews can influence identity, values or choices.

Forty minute route

Arrival 4; starter 3; model 6; shared task 7; check 2; independent 12; review 3; exit 3 minutes. Pause time is flexible.

Preparation

Print the glue-in strips, the evidence and shared cards, the required visual or data sheet and the route card. Exits go in books.

Keep the answers with staff. Use fictional source profiles and object cards; no personal objects, beliefs or experiences are required.

Access and regulation

Offer a predictable start, private response and agreed pause. No cold calling or forced personal disclosure. Rejoin at one clearly named next step. Keep teen-appropriate examples and the same learning goal across response modes.

This is learning about religion and worldviews, not worship. Nobody is asked to share a personal belief, family detail or loss.

Assessment

Collect six answers, including a short extended comparison and the new key idea in books. Keep the RAG private. Record normal access support separately.

UAS: staff must match evidence to the centre-selected unit and its exact criteria; this lesson makes no automatic award claim.

First lesson back · staff card

Book scan

Scan a small sample of retained Autumn 1 work for a source detail, a reason and feedback codes. Unclosed next steps from the cover period are history: do not chase them.

Ask cover staff and TAs

  1. Which key idea was taught and what did pupils show?
  2. Which earlier idea could pupils explain independently?
  3. Which access support worked for private responses?

Once-only return line

I haven't seen what you've been doing… I start from what you show me.

Today

Use the Autumn 1 Week 7 model for belief and identity evidence. Teach the key idea, then collect the short individual check in books. Begin from what pupils show today.

Private RAG rule

Green: selects relevant evidence and explains a belief-to-choice link; earlier examples and the comparison are accurate. Amber: evidence is relevant but a causal link or earlier idea needs a prompt. Red: needs direct teaching to distinguish a claim, evidence and explanation. A reader or exact scribe does not lower the RAG; record access support separately.

What the check feeds into

Use the private RAG and exact access support to choose the next lesson’s opening example and Supported, Standard or Stretch route. Give one feedback code and one next step. Do not read scores aloud.

Planned adaptations

Broad areaEEF five-a-day strategy and adaptation
Cognition and learningExplicit instruction; scaffolding: Model a point, relevant evidence and explanation separately. Chunk the extended comparison into a point, one detail from each source, and a because link; withdraw the model during the individual check.
Communication and interactionScaffolding; flexible grouping: Pre-teach the key words with the source pictures. Offer silent planning, partner rehearsal, pointing, typing or exact scribing before an individual response.
SEMHCognitive and metacognitive strategies; flexible grouping: Use the predictable nine-stage routine, private feedback and an agreed pause. Keep fictional examples, allow a pass on public speaking, and rejoin at one named step.
Sensory and physicalUsing technology; scaffolding: Offer the normal enlarged print, read-aloud, typing, pointing or adapted grip. Use the manual model controls and reduce motion; assess the RE idea rather than handwriting.
EAL (EAL is not SEN)Explicit instruction; scaffolding: Pre-teach the lesson vocabulary with an image and example, allow first-language planning, and distinguish language access from conceptual understanding.

Target opportunities

Capture E against the pupil's own IEDP target on the school's evidence app; the IEDP carries their EHCP-linked and Boxall targets, so one record serves every plan. Follow the pupil's IBSP where it differs from these routines.

Record communication in a pupil’s own explanation, cognition in a revised source link, regulation in an agreed pause and return, or sensory/physical access where it matches the individual target. Record only what was observed.

Book evidence and feedback

At Independent, one adult supports access while the other holds the group; swap across the week. Read or scribe the pupil’s exact response without choosing an answer.

VF: verbal feedback. WS: with support; record the prompt. I: independent response. NS+: one precise next step in a yellow box. E: evidence against the pupil’s own target on the school’s evidence app. R: a response after Voice, Audience and NS+. //: self-edit. ?: read back.

At Review, read back one response (?), offer one precise next step, allow a // edit and recheck. At Exit, pass the private route decision and access support to the next lesson.

Teaching sequence

Arrival: collect answers before revealing. Starter: retrieve the three earlier ideas. I do: teach the source model. We do: physically match cards and explain a placement. Hinge: collect the letter and clue privately. Independent: use the agreed route for each short check item. Review: use ? and // to improve one detail. Exit: explain the key idea privately.

Arrival questions and answers

How did Daniel’s belief influence his work? He believes everyone deserves dignity, so chose care work.

What makes evidence relevant? It directly answers the question being asked.

Name a source of authority in RE. A sacred text, conscience or tradition can guide a person.

Must everyone write the same amount? No. Use the agreed access route; the quality of the idea matters.

Starter answers

Define a worldview. The way a person sees life and what matters.

What does authority mean in RE? A source people trust to guide what they believe or do.

What does an explanation add to a list? It says how or why, using because or therefore.

Shared activity reasoning

Daniel chose care work — Belief influencing a choice — Dignity → care work.

Priya: “I want my life to be useful” — Belief influencing identity — How she sees herself.

Amira turns to the Qur’an on honesty — Authority influencing values — A sacred text guides her.

Hinge and diagnoses

Which detail is most relevant to explaining how Daniel’s belief influences his work?

B. He chose care work because he believes everyone deserves dignity. It explicitly links Daniel’s belief in dignity to his job choice.

A: Selects a detail without linking it to the question.

C: Gives background without explaining this influence.

D: Overgeneralises from one fictional profile.

Parallel hinge after a teaching move

Priya believes this is our one life and volunteers as a mentor. Which detail explains the influence?

A. She wants this life to be useful, so chooses to mentor others. It links her belief to a value and a choice.

If time is short

Keep the taught key idea, individual check, one review improvement and exit. Shorten extra matching turns or repeated playback. Do not let recording length hide understanding.

Planning and evaluation record

Date taught: ____________________

Delivered as planned: Yes / Partly / No

Criteria met: all / most / some

Adaptations and reason: ____________________

Evidence captured and next lesson’s move: ____________________

Keep answers with staff.

Hide the model during independent assessment.

Individual check answers and source map

  1. Earlier learning: Identity and choice. He chose care work because he believes everyone deserves dignity; the work lets him act on this belief. Source: Autumn 1 Week 1.
  2. Earlier learning: Two worldviews. For example, Christians believe in one God as Trinity; Humanists do not believe in a god and regard this as our only life. Their beliefs about God differ. Source: Autumn 1 Week 2.
  3. Earlier learning: Authority. A trusted source of guidance. Amira may use the Qur’an to guide honesty; a person may consult conscience about right and wrong. Source: Autumn 1 Week 3.
  4. Earlier learning: Shared values. Peace, welcome or dialogue. Mediation helps neighbours resolve conflict; the open day helps neighbours meet. Source: Autumn 1 Week 4.
  5. Earlier learning: Explaining. “For example, he chose care work” is evidence; the last sentence links that choice to the value of dignity and explains how. Source: Autumn 1 Week 5.
  6. Earlier learning: Extended response. Both remember people and value peace. The Christian source prays and believes people are in God’s care; the Humanist source does not pray and values memories and preventing war. They share remembrance and hope for peace while their beliefs and practices differ. Source: Autumn 1 Week 6.

Exit guidance

Daniel believes everyone deserves dignity and chose care work. His job choice directly supports the claim that belief can influence choices. Priya and volunteering are an equally valid source-based example.

staff_sections.heading: Individual check answers and source map
staff_sections.html:
1. Earlier learning: Identity and choice. He chose care work because he believes everyone deserves dignity; the work lets him act on this belief. Source: Autumn 1 Week 1.
  2. Earlier learning: Two worldviews. For example, Christians believe in one God as Trinity; Humanists do not believe in a god and regard this as our only life. Their beliefs about God differ. Source: Autumn 1 Week 2.
  3. Earlier learning: Authority. A trusted source of guidance. Amira may use the Qur’an to guide honesty; a person may consult conscience about right and wrong. Source: Autumn 1 Week 3.
  4. Earlier learning: Shared values. Peace, welcome or dialogue. Mediation helps neighbours resolve conflict; the open day helps neighbours meet. Source: Autumn 1 Week 4.
  5. Earlier learning: Explaining. “For example, he chose care work” is evidence; the last sentence links that choice to the value of dignity and explains how. Source: Autumn 1 Week 5.
  6. Earlier learning: Extended response. Both remember people and value peace. The Christian source prays and believes people are in God’s care; the Humanist source does not pray and values memories and preventing war. They share remembrance and hope for peace while their beliefs and practices differ. Source: Autumn 1 Week 6.

LAUNCH · RE & World Views · Autumn 1 · Week 8

Short individual book check

In your book: Answer 1 to 5 briefly; use point, evidence and explanation for 6.

Work quietly in your own book. A reader, word bank or exact scribe is available on every route.

Supported

Read one prompt at a time. Use the word bank. For 6, dictate or complete point, evidence, explain.

  1. Identity and choice. Daniel believes everyone deserves dignity. Explain how this influences his choice of work.
  2. Two worldviews. Give one key belief in Christianity and one in Humanism, then identify a difference.
  3. Authority. What is authority in RE? Explain how a sacred text or conscience could guide a choice.

return_check.prompt: Daniel believes everyone deserves dignity. Explain how this influences his choice of work.
return_check.answer: He chose care work because he believes everyone deserves dignity; the work lets him act on this belief.

source_lessons.outcome: Explain one way a belief or worldview can influence a person's identity or choices.

return_check.prompt: Give one key belief in Christianity and one in Humanism, then identify a difference.
return_check.answer: For example, Christians believe in one God as Trinity; Humanists do not believe in a god and regard this as our only life. Their beliefs about God differ.

source_lessons.outcome: Identify a key belief in two worldviews and explain one similarity or difference.

return_check.prompt: What is authority in RE? Explain how a sacred text or conscience could guide a choice.
return_check.answer: A trusted source of guidance. Amira may use the Qur’an to guide honesty; a person may consult conscience about right and wrong.

source_lessons.outcome: Recognise a source of authority or meaning and explain how it may guide a believer or non- religious person.

return_check.prompt: Name a shared value shown by the church mediation group and the mosque open day. Give a source detail.
return_check.answer: Peace, welcome or dialogue. Mediation helps neighbours resolve conflict; the open day helps neighbours meet.

source_lessons.outcome: Explain how a festival or shared value can bring people together and identify one value linked to peace.

return_check.prompt: In “Daniel values dignity. For example, he chose care work. This lets him care for others”, identify the evidence and explain what the final sentence adds.
return_check.answer: “For example, he chose care work” is evidence; the last sentence links that choice to the value of dignity and explains how.

source_lessons.outcome: Write or give a structured explanation using a point, evidence/example and explanation.

return_check.prompt: Compare the Christian and Humanist remembrance responses. Use a point, a detail from each source and an explanation of a similarity and a difference.
return_check.answer: Both remember people and value peace. The Christian source prays and believes people are in God’s care; the Humanist source does not pray and values memories and preventing war. They share remembrance and hope for peace while their beliefs and practices differ.

source_lessons.outcome: Compare how two worldviews may respond to remembrance or peace.

source_map.title: Belief, identity and belonging in adult life
source_map.outcome: Explain one way a belief or worldview can influence a person's identity or choices.
model: Question: How does Daniel’s belief influence his choice of work?

Evidence: A Daniel: Fictional profile: Daniel is 24, Christian and a care worker. He says, “I believe every person is made in the image of God, so everyone deserves dignity.” He chose care work over a better-paid job.
Think aloud: He believes everyone deserves dignity, so he chose care work.
Check: Does a belief fully determine a person’s identity? No. It is one influence among several, and views can change.

cards.title: Daniel
cards.text: Fictional profile: Daniel is 24, Christian and a care worker. He says, “I believe every person is made in the image of God, so everyone deserves dignity.” He chose care work over a better-paid job.
cards.limit: This is one person's view. Others who share the worldview may describe it differently.

cards.title: Priya
cards.text: Fictional profile: Priya is 26 and a Humanist. She says, “This is the one life we have, so I want mine to be useful.” She volunteers as a mentor and gives blood.
cards.limit: This is one person's view. Others who share the worldview may describe it differently.

cards.title: Belief → choice → identity
cards.text: A belief can lead to a choice. Repeated choices become part of how a person sees themselves and how others see them.
cards.limit: Real lives are less tidy than a three-step model.

cards.title: Other influences
cards.text: Family, money, health, friends and place also shape adult choices. Belief is one influence, and people can change their views.
cards.limit: Belief does not fully determine identity.

words: The way a person sees life and what matters
To have an effect on something
What a person thinks is important in how to live
Who a person is and how they see themselves

source_map.title: Key beliefs across two worldviews
source_map.outcome: Identify a key belief in two worldviews and explain one similarity or difference.
model: Question: Name one belief from each worldview.

Evidence: A Christianity: key beliefs: Christians believe in one God, understood as Trinity. They believe Jesus is the Son of God, and that his teaching and example show how to live. Most believe in life after death. B Humanism: key beliefs: Humanists do not believe in a god. They hold that this life is the only one we have, that reason and evidence are the best guides, and that people can live good lives without religion.
Think aloud: For example: Christians believe in God as Trinity; Humanists believe this is our only life.
Check: Do all Christians believe exactly the same things? No. Use “some”, “many” or “most”.

cards.title: Christianity: key beliefs
cards.text: Christians believe in one God, understood as Trinity. They believe Jesus is the Son of God, and that his teaching and example show how to live. Most believe in life after death.
cards.limit: Christians differ on many details.

cards.title: Humanism: key beliefs
cards.text: Humanists do not believe in a god. They hold that this life is the only one we have, that reason and evidence are the best guides, and that people can live good lives without religion.
cards.source: Authored summary of Humanists UK’s description of Humanism
cards.limit: Humanists differ on many details.

cards.title: Belief or practice?
cards.text: A belief is held to be true: “God exists.” A practice is done: “going to church”. Compare belief with belief.
cards.limit: Some statements mix both.

cards.title: Shared ground
cards.text: Both worldviews value kindness, honesty and responsibility for others. They differ on God and on life after death.
cards.limit: Sharing values does not make two worldviews the same.

words: A person who believes in God or gods
Not following a religion, but still holding beliefs and values
A non-religious worldview based on reason, evidence and care for others
The Christian belief in one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit

source_map.title: Sources of authority and meaning
source_map.outcome: Recognise a source of authority or meaning and explain how it may guide a believer or non- religious person.
model: Question: Define “authority” in RE.
Evidence: C Authority is not “being in charge”: A boss can give orders. An authority in RE is a source a person chooses to trust for guidance.
Think aloud: A source people trust to guide what they believe or do.
Check: Is authority in RE the same as being in charge? No. It is a trusted source of guidance.

cards.title: Religious sources
cards.text: Many believers turn to sacred texts, religious leaders such as a priest, imam or rabbi, and the traditions of their community.
cards.limit: Belief and practice vary between individuals and communities.

cards.title: Non-religious sources
cards.text: Many non-religious people turn to reason, evidence, conscience and the experience of people they trust.
cards.limit: Religious people use reason and conscience too.

cards.title: Authority is not “being in charge”
cards.text: A boss can give orders. An authority in RE is a source a person chooses to trust for guidance.
cards.limit: People can question an authority and still respect it.

cards.title: Scenarios
cards.text: Amira must decide whether to report a friend who is stealing at work. Joe must decide whether to take a job that means working every Sunday.
cards.limit: This example does not describe every person, family or community.

words: A source people trust to guide what they believe or do
Writing that is holy to a religion, such as the Bible or the Qur’an
A person’s inner sense of right and wrong
Beliefs and practices passed down over time

source_map.title: Festivals, shared values and the Day of Peace
source_map.outcome: Explain how a festival or shared value can bring people together and identify one value linked to peace.
model: Question: Name one value shared across two worldviews.

Evidence: B A Christian example: Jesus taught “Blessed are the peacemakers”. Fictional case: a church runs a mediation group for neighbours in dispute. C A Muslim example: The greeting “As-salamu alaykum” means “peace be upon you”. Fictional case: a mosque hosts an open day so neighbours can meet.
Think aloud: For example, peace, welcome or dialogue.
Check: Is the Day of Peace only for religious people? No. It is for everyone.

cards.title: The Day of Peace
cards.text: The United Nations International Day of Peace is held on 21 September each year. It invites everyone, of any worldview, to act for peace.
cards.source: Authored summary of the United Nations observance
cards.limit: A day of peace does not end conflict. It asks people to act.

cards.title: A Christian example
cards.text: Jesus taught “Blessed are the peacemakers”. Fictional case: a church runs a mediation group for neighbours in dispute.
cards.limit: Belief and practice vary between individuals and communities.

cards.title: A Muslim example
cards.text: The greeting “As-salamu alaykum” means “peace be upon you”. Fictional case: a mosque hosts an open day so neighbours can meet.
cards.limit: Belief and practice vary between individuals and communities.

cards.title: A Humanist example
cards.text: Humanists argue that peace comes through reason, dialogue and human rights. Fictional case: a Humanist group runs a schools debate on resolving conflict.
cards.limit: Belief and practice vary between individuals and communities.

words: Something people of different worldviews agree is important
When people are safe and conflicts are settled without violence
Something that stands for an idea
People linked by a place, belief or activity

source_map.title: A structured “explain” response
source_map.outcome: Write or give a structured explanation using a point, evidence/example and explanation.
model: Question: In the model answer, which sentence is the evidence?

Evidence: C A model explanation: “A belief can influence a person’s work. For example, Daniel believes everyone deserves dignity. Therefore he chose care work, because it lets him act on that belief.”
Think aloud: “For example, Daniel believes everyone deserves dignity.”
Check: Is a list the same as an explanation? No. An explanation says how or why.

cards.title: The structure
cards.text: Point: answer the question. Evidence or example: “For example…”. Explain: “This shows… because…”. Three sentences are enough.
cards.limit: This is a support for clear thinking, not an exam technique.

cards.title: A list, not an explanation
cards.text: “Christians pray, go to church and read the Bible.” This lists. It never says why.
cards.limit: A list can be the start of a good answer.

cards.title: A model explanation
cards.text: “A belief can influence a person’s work. For example, Daniel believes everyone deserves dignity. Therefore he chose care work, because it lets him act on that belief.”
cards.limit: A model shows the method. Other good answers exist.

cards.title: Question bank
cards.text: How can a belief influence a choice? Why might someone trust a sacred text? How can a shared value bring people together?
cards.limit: Choose the question you can support with evidence.

words: A clear answer to the question
An example or fact that supports the point
To say how or why, using “because” or “therefore”
A word that shows what follows from the evidence

source_map.title: Remembrance and peace across beliefs
source_map.outcome: Compare how two worldviews may respond to remembrance or peace.
model: Question: Give one similarity or difference between the two responses.

Evidence: B A Christian response: Fictional source: “At our service we pray for those who died and for peace. I believe they are in God’s care, which gives me hope.” C A Humanist response: Fictional source: “I don’t pray, but I stand in silence. People live on in what they did and in our memories. Remembering should make us work to prevent war.”
Think aloud: For example: both keep silence, but only the Christian source prays.
Check: Is classroom reflection the same as worship? No. It is quiet thinking.

cards.title: Remembrance in the UK
cards.text: On Remembrance Sunday and 11 November many people keep two minutes of silence. The poppy is a symbol of remembrance and of hope for a peaceful future.
cards.source: Authored summary; see Royal British Legion, The poppy
cards.limit: Wearing a poppy is a personal choice.

cards.title: A Christian response
cards.text: Fictional source: “At our service we pray for those who died and for peace. I believe they are in God’s care, which gives me hope.”
cards.limit: This is one person's view. Others who share the worldview may describe it differently.

cards.title: A Humanist response
cards.text: Fictional source: “I don’t pray, but I stand in silence. People live on in what they did and in our memories. Remembering should make us work to prevent war.”
cards.limit: This is one person's view. Others who share the worldview may describe it differently.

cards.title: Reflection is not worship
cards.text: In class, reflection is quiet thinking. Nobody is asked to pray or to share a personal loss.
cards.limit: A quiet alternative is always available.

words: Taking time to remember people and events
Quiet thinking about something that matters
To look for similarities and differences
Something made to help people remember

first_lesson_back_html:
First lesson back · staff card

Book scan

Scan a small sample of retained Autumn 1 work for a source detail, a reason and feedback codes. Unclosed next steps from the cover period are history: do not chase them.

Ask cover staff and TAs

  1. Which key idea was taught and what did pupils show?
  2. Which earlier idea could pupils explain independently?
  3. Which access support worked for private responses?

Once-only return line

I haven't seen what you've been doing… I start from what you show me.

Today

Use the Autumn 1 Week 7 model for belief and identity evidence. Teach the key idea, then collect the short individual check in books. Begin from what pupils show today.

Private RAG rule

Green: selects relevant evidence and explains a belief-to-choice link; earlier examples and the comparison are accurate. Amber: evidence is relevant but a causal link or earlier idea needs a prompt. Red: needs direct teaching to distinguish a claim, evidence and explanation. A reader or exact scribe does not lower the RAG; record access support separately.

What the check feeds into

Use the private RAG and exact access support to choose the next lesson’s opening example and Supported, Standard or Stretch route. Give one feedback code and one next step. Do not read scores aloud.
